doc.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002

chapter: Richmond and arriving in New York
title: Learning the standards repertoire
summary: New York forced him to build his repertoire; singers sometimes call tunes in odd keys.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: That tradition of kind of getting into jam sessions and hopefully proving yourself has been around for a long time. In the late eighties was the repertoire that you’re expected to know, was it still the standards?

Oh yeah. And that was probably one of the first things that hit me when I moved to New York was having to learn those standards or re-learn them. I had been learning some of these tunes, some of the Monk tunes and some of the tunes of the American Songbook before I moved there but man these musicians, these young musicians knew all of these tunes inside and out. So it really forced me to build my repertoire and it was very healthy to do that. It forced me to do it.
Did anybody ever call things like in non-standard keys?
Occasionally yeah. It didn’t happen too much but when I started working with vocalists.
And then of course they’ll call “All the Things You Are” in F, instead of A flat. Oh yeah, what’s the first chord. So yeah.
